input.title: John 9
input.description: John 9 in the Liberation and Inclusion Translation (LIT).
topics: who sinned, this man or his parents?
I am the light of the world
I was blind but now I see
paragraphs: 1 As he passed by, he saw a person who had been blind from birth. 2 His students asked him, “Rabbi, who deviated to cause him to be born blind: this person or his parents?”

3 “Neither this person nor his parents deviated,” Jesus answered. “Just the opposite, it has the result thata what God seeks to accomplishb can be clearly shown with him.c 4 It is necessary for us to work toward what the one who sent me seeks to accomplish as long as it is daytime. Night is coming when no one can work. 5 While I’m in the world, I am the light of the world.”
6 After he said these things, he spit on the ground and made mudd from the saliva. He spread the mud on the blind man’se eyes.
7 “Go,” Jesus said to him, “Wash in the pool of Siloam” (which is translated as ‘sent’). Then the blind manf went away and washed, and he came back seeing.
8 Then neighbors and the people who saw him previously because he had needed to request people give him things to surviveg started saying, “Isn’t this the person who used to sit and ask for things?”
9 Some were saying, “This is him!”
Others were saying, “No, but he looks like him.”
The man kept saying, “It’s me!”h
10 So they started asking him, “Then, how were your eyes opened?”
11 “The man called Jesus,” he answered, “made mud and spread it on my eyes, and he told me, ‘Go to Siloam and wash.’ So, I left, and after I washed, I could use my eyes.”i
12 “Where is that man?” they said to him.
“I don’t know,” he said.

13 They brought the man who used to be blind to the Pharisees 14 (It was Shabbat on the day Jesus made mud and opened his eyes). 15 Then the Pharisees were the ones who asked him again how had been able to use his eyes.
“He put mud on my eyes,” he told them, “And I washed, and I could see.”

16 Then some of the Pharisees started saying, “This person is not from God because he doesn’t carefully observe Shabbat,” but others were saying, “How can a person who is deviating produce signs like these?” and there was a split between them.
17 Then they said to the formerlyj blind man again, “What do you say about him, since he opened your eyes?”
“He is a prophet,” he said.

18 So the Judean authorities didn’t trust the claim about him that he had been blind and then able to use his eyes until they had called the parents of the one who had become able to use his eyes, 19 and they asked them.
“Is this your son,” they said, “About whom you say, ‘He was born blind’? Then, how is he seeing right now?”

20 Then his parents answered. “We know that this is our son and that he was born blind,” they said. 21 “But we don’t know how he can see now. Ask him. He’s old enough. He’ll speak for himself.” 22 (His parents said this because they were afraid of the Judean authorities. You see, the Judean authorities had already agreed together that if anyone acknowledged him as Christ, they would become expelled from the synagogue.k 23 That’s why his parents said, “He’s old enough. Ask him.”)
24 Then they called for the person who had been blind a second time.
“Contribute to God’s praise!”l they said to him. “We know that this person is a deviator.”
25 “I don’t know whether he is a deviator,” he answered. “I know one thing, that although I used to be blind, now I can see.”
26 “What did he do to you?” they said. “How did he open your eyes?”
27 “I already told you, and you didn’t listen!” he said. “You don’t want to become his students too, do you?”
28 They verbally attacked him and said, “You are that man’s student, but we are Moses’ students! 29 We know that God has spoken to Moses, but we don’t know where this man is from.”

30 “Well, that’s what makes it amazing, that you don’t know where he’s from, yet he opened my eyes!” the man said to them. 31 “We know that God does not listen to deviators, but if someone is respectful of God so that they do what he wants, then God listens. 32 Since ages past,m it has not been heard that anyone born blind has had their eyes opened. 33 Unless this man were from God, he wouldn’t be able to do anything.”
34 They responded to him, “You were born entirely coveredn with deviations, yet you’re teaching us!” and they expelled him from the community.o
35 Jesus heard that they expelled him from the community,p and after going to find him, he said, “Have you placed your trust in the Son of Humanity?”
36 “Who is he, sir?” he answered, “so I can place my trust in him?”
37 “You have seen him,” Jesus said, “and he is the one who is speaking with you.”
⟦ 38 So he said, “I trust, Lord,” and he bowed down to him.
39 Jesus said, ⟧q “I came to the world for justice,r so those who can’t see would see and those who can see would become blind.”
40 The Pharisees who were with him heard this and said, “We aren’t blind too, are we?”
41 “If you were blind,” Jesus told them, “You wouldn’t have deviation. But now that you say, ‘We can see,’ your deviation stays present.”

footnotes.label: a
footnotes.html: The Greek word hina can be translated a number of ways. It’s simplest translation is ‘so that.’ However, it can be used to indicate a cause, a purpose, a result, and other related ideas. The traditional translations word it in such a way that shows the translators take it to be about purpose. However, that assumption does not fit Jesus’ teaching. The most natural way to translate this so that it fits with Jesus’ teaching is to understand it as being about result, not purpose. It then is simply something that happened, not that God caused to prove a point, and it is being used as an opportunity to treat the person how God would treat them.

footnotes.label: b
footnotes.html: Compare with John 8:39, 41. Literally, ‘the work/actions of God.’

footnotes.label: c
footnotes.html: The context makes clear that this story is about Jesus and his students, not about the blind man. If the blind man is the subject, then God is unjust, causing him and his parents suffering and hardship throughout his whole life (up to this point and beyond since while he can see after this story, he still has to start from scratch with building a life) just to prove a point. That perspective does not fit with Jesus’ message. Jesus sees an opportunity to model what God cares about and how people who follow the path of the Lord are responsible to treat others. Jesus does whatever is in his power to improve a stranger’s life. He teaches his students to do the same. That is what it means to do ‘the work of God.’ It happens with this blind man, and it’s intended to spread and become the default way of life for those who follow Jesus. The rest of the chapter shows how people wrestled with understanding what Jesus’ actions demonstrated about God.

footnotes.label: d
footnotes.html: Or ‘wet clay’

footnotes.label: e
footnotes.html: Literally, ‘his.’

footnotes.label: f
footnotes.html: Literally, ‘he’

footnotes.label: g
footnotes.html: The Greek word prosaites traditionally has been translated as ‘beggar.’ In present culture, a term like that would be accompanied by judgment and dismissal. It is not appropriate to use a term like that in the narrative of Jesus’ story. It has been translated here with a long, descriptive phrase, essentially a whole definition rather than a single term: ‘someone who needs to request people give them things to survive.’

footnotes.label: h
footnotes.html: Literally, ‘I am,’ the same Greek Jesus uses (ego eimi) to state “I AM before Abraham’s existence” (John 8:58) and let his students know it was him walking on water: “Take courage! I AM me! Don’t be afraid” (Matthew 14:27).

footnotes.label: i
footnotes.html: Literally, ‘look up.’ Jesus uses the same word as a direction to his students in John 4:35, telling them to ‘use your eyes’ or ‘look up.’

footnotes.label: j
footnotes.html: The word ‘formerly’ is not in the Greek. It just says “Then they said to the blind again.”

footnotes.label: k
footnotes.html: The Greek is aposunagogos genetai, literally, ‘become away-from-synagogue.’ The word ‘synagogue’ is from the Greek sunagoge, which means ‘gathered together,’ or ‘community gathering.’ They were worried about being excommunicated, banished from the community life and worship. This is a different wording than John 9:34–35, though it is a related concept, probably even meaning the same action.

footnotes.label: l
footnotes.html: This short sentence was an idiom used as way of placing the man under oath. It was essentially, “Stop lying and reflect God by telling the truth instead.”

footnotes.label: m
footnotes.html: Literally, ‘from the ages…’

footnotes.label: n
footnotes.html: The word ‘covered’ is not in the Greek but is used to make the thought flow more smoothly in English. A more literal translation would be something like “All of you was born with deviations.”

footnotes.label: o
footnotes.html: The words ‘from the community’ are not in the Greek, but it is certainly what was in view, not just telling him to leave the building for that moment. He was kicked out of membership and participation in Jewish community life and worship (he was excommunicated). The Greek phrase is exebalon auton exo (literally, ‘they threw him out outside.’ There is an extra emphasis on the ‘out’ or ‘outside.’ The verb exebalon (root: ekballo) already means ‘throw out’ or ‘cast out’ or ‘banish.’ It is a compound of ek (preposition meaning ‘out of’ or ‘out from’) and ballo (to throw, to project). The word exo is related to the preposition and means ‘outside’ or ‘out.’ John 9:22 explained that the Pharisees had decided to expel people from the community if they acknowledged Jesus as Christ. It uses a different phrase in that verse: aposunagogos genetai, literally, ‘become away-from-synagogue.’ The word ‘synagogue’ is from the Greek sunagoge, which means ‘gathered together,’ or ‘community gathering.’ The book of John seems to use ekballo exo (‘throw out outside/banish outside’) the way Matthew uses ekballo eis to skotos to exoteron (‘throw out into the outer darkness’).

footnotes.label: p
footnotes.html: Again, ‘from the synagogue’ is not in the Greek, but the phrasing is about being kicked out of the community, not just escorted out of the building.

footnotes.label: q
footnotes.html: The earliest and most reliable manuscripts don’t include verse 38 and the part of verse 39 that says, “Jesus said.”

footnotes.label: r
footnotes.html: Most of the instances of ‘assessment’ or what is traditionally translated as ‘judgment’ are krisis, but the word here is krima. Both words can be used in a number of ways, but in John, krisis usually refers to something like ‘the process or result of assessing/deciding,’ i.e. ‘assessment’ or ‘decision,’ and krima seems to be the equivalent of the Hebrew mishpat (and was used to translate it in the Septuagint), which is about justice in which the poor and oppressed are given equity. BDAG includes one of the definitions as “proper recognition of someone’s rights, justice.” It is restitutionary and restorative justice in action, not retributive justice. It’s about supporting those who have been wronged or marginalized, not punishing bad behavior.

The Greek phrase is exebalon auton exo (literally, ‘they threw him out outside.’ There is an extra emphasis on the ‘out’ or ‘outside.’ The verb exebalon (root: ekballo) already means ‘throw out’ or ‘cast out’ or ‘banish.’ It is a compound of ek (preposition meaning ‘out of’ or ‘out from’) and ballo (to throw, to project). The word exo is related to the preposition and means ‘outside’ or ‘out.’ John 9:22 explained that the Pharisees had decided to expel people from the community if they acknowledged Jesus as Christ. It uses a different phrase in that verse: aposunagogos genetai, literally, ‘become away-from-synagogue.’ The word ‘synagogue’ is from the Greek sunagoge, which means ‘gathered together,’ or ‘community gathering.’ The book of John seems to use ekballo exo (‘throw out outside/banish outside’) the way Matthew uses ekballo eis to skotos to exoteron (‘throw out into the outer darkness’).

footnotes.label: r
footnotes.html: Most of the instances of ‘assessment’ or what is traditionally translated as ‘judgment’ are krisis, but the word here is krima. Both words can be used in a number of ways, but in John, krisis usually refers to something like ‘the process or result of assessing/deciding,’ i.e. ‘assessment’ or ‘decision,’ and krima seems to be the equivalent of the Hebrew mishpat (and was used to translate it in the Septuagint), which is about justice in which the poor and oppressed are given equity. BDAG includes one of the definitions as “proper recognition of someone’s rights, justice.” It is restitutionary and restorative justice in action, not retributive justice. It’s about supporting those who have been wronged or marginalized, not punishing bad behavior.

input.description: John 11 in the Liberation and Inclusion Translation (LIT).
topics: I am the resurrection and the life
paragraphs: 1 There was someone who was weak with illness, Eleazara from Bethany,b which was the village where Miriamc and her sister Marthad were from 2 (Miriam was the one who anointed the Lord with perfumed oil and wiped his feet with her hair and whose brother Eleazar was weak with illness). 3 So, Miriam sent a message for Jesuse: “Lord,f the one you care aboutg is weak with illness.”

4 When he heard it, Jesus replied to her, “This illness isn’t resulting in death, but for the sake of praiseh for God with the result that the Son of God would be praisedi because of it.”j 5 (Jesus lovedk Martha and her sister and Eleazer). 6 So, after he heard he was weak with illness, he stayed where he was for two more days.
7 Then, after that, he said to his students, “We should go back to Judea.”
8 “Rabbi,” his students said to him, “just now, the Judean authorities were trying to stone you to death! And you want to go back there?”

9 “Aren’t there 12 hours during the day?” Jesus answered. “If someone walks during the day, they don’t run into anything since they see the light of this world. 10 But if someone walks during the night, they run into things since the light is not with them.”
11 He said these things, and later he told them, “Our friendl Eleazar has fallen asleep;m however, I am traveling there so I can wake him up.”

12 So his students said to him, “Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he’ll be restored from his illness”n 13 (Jesus had been talking about his death, but they thought he was talking about resting in sleep).
14 So then Jesus told them openly, “Eleazar died, 15 and I’m glad for your sake that I wasn’t there, so you can trust me, but we should go to him.”
16 Then Thomaso (called Didymusp) said to his fellow students, “We should go too, so we can die with him.”

17 When Jesus arrived, he found Eleazarq already had been within the tomb for four days. 18 (Bethany was near Jerusalem, less than two milesr away. 19 Many Judeans had come to [Martha and] Miriam to console her regarding her brother.) 20 So, when [Martha] heard Jesus was coming while Miriam was sitting in her house, she went to go meet him.
21 Then [Martha] said to Jesus, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother wouldn’t have died. 22 However, I know even now whatever you ask God for, God will give it to you.”
23 “Your brother will rise up,”s Jesus told her.
24 “I know he will rise up at the rising up on the last day,” [Martha] said.

25 “I am the rising upt and life,” Jesus said to her. “Whoever places their trust in me will live even if they die, 26 and everyone who is alive and places their trust in me certainly won’t die throughout the Age. Do you trust this?”
27 “Yes, Lord,” she said, “I have trusted that you are the Christ, God’s Son who has come tou the whole world.”v

⟦28 After she said this, she went and discretely called her sister Miriam. “The teacher has arrived and is calling for you,” she said. 29 When Miriamw heard, she got up quickly and went to him. 30 (Jesus had not yet gone into the village but was still in the place where Martha met with him.) 31 Then, the Judeans who were with her in the house consoling her followed her after they saw Miriam get up quickly and leave because they thought she was going to the tomb to mournx there. 32 Then, when Miriam arrived at the place where Jesus was and saw him, she collapsed at his feet. “Lord,” she said to him, “If you had been here, my brother wouldn’t have died!” ⟧y
33 Then, as Jesus saw her mourning and the Judeans who had come with her mourning, he angrily confronted himselfz in the spirit and worked himself upaa 34 and said, “Where have you laid him?”
“Lord,” they told him, “Come and see.”
35 Jesus wept.bb
36 Then the Judeans began saying, “Look how much he cared about him!”
37 However, some of them said, “Wasn’t hecc—since he opened the eyes of the blind man—able to make it so that Eleazardd wouldn’t die?”
38 Then, Jesus—angrily confronting himselfee again—arrived at the tomb. (It was a cave, and a stone was laid over the opening.)
39 “Lift the stone away,” Jesus said.
[Martha], the sister of the deceased, told him, “Lord, he already smells since it’s the fourth day.”
40 “Didn’t I tell you that if you trusted, you would see God’s praiseworthiness?” Jesus responded. 41 So they lifted away the stone.

Jesus looked up and said, “Father, I give thanks to you because you listened to me. 42 I had learned that you always listen to me, but for the sake of the people standing here I said it aloud so that they can trust that you sent me.”

43 After he said these things, he shouted with a loud voice, “Eleazar, come out here!”ff 44 The one who had died came out, still having his feet and hands bound with strips of cloth and a cloth wrapped around his face. “Remove the binding and let him go,” Jesus told them.

45 Then many of the Judeans who had come with Miriam and seen the things he did placed their trust in him. 46 But some of them went to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus did. 47 So the lead priests and Pharisees gathered the councilgg together and began saying, “What do we do about this person producing so many signs? 48 If we let him go on like this, everyone will place their trust in him, and the Romans will come and take away our place and our people!”

49 Then one of them, Caiaphas who was the high priest that year, said to them, “You don’t know anything! 50 You haven’t even figured out that it benefits you that one person would die for the sake of the whole populationhh and not the whole peopleii be destroyed. 51 (He didn’t say this by himself, but rather, as high priest for that year, he prophesied that Jesus was going to die for the sake of the people,jj 52 and not for the sake of that people only but so that God’s children who were scattered would be gathered into one.kk) 53 So, from that day on, they planned together that they would kill him.
54 So, Jesus didn’t travel in Judea openly anymore; instead, he went from that region to the area near the Wilderness, to a town called Ephraim, and he stayed there with the students.

55 It was almost the Jewish festival, Passover, and many people went up to Jerusalem from the countryside before Passover so that they could prepare themselves for religious participation,ll 56 so the lead priests and Phariseesmm were looking for Jesus.

As they stood in the sacred grounds, they were saying to each other, “What do you think? That it’s certain he won’t come to the festival?” 57 (The lead priests and Pharisees had given directions that if someone learned where he was, they should report it, so they could capture him.)

footnotes.label: a
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘Lazarus.’ I have chosen to allow the Jewishness of the people described in these writings to be evident by using the names that are connected with the Hebrew origins when they are Hebrew-derived names instead of being double translated through Greek. ‘Eleazar’ in Hebrew means ‘the one whom God helps.’

footnotes.label: b
footnotes.html: Bethany was in Judea, the area he just left to escape the authorities who were trying to kill him.

footnotes.label: c
footnotes.html: Christian tradition has translated this name as ‘Mary.’ The Greek Mariam is a translation of the Hebrew name ‘Miriam.’ I have chosen to allow the Jewishness of the people described in these writings to be evident by using the names that are connected with the Hebrew origins when they are Hebrew-derived names instead of being double translated through Greek.

footnotes.label: d
footnotes.html: Or, ‘and his sister Miriam.’ Recent research into the oldest available manuscript of John, Papyrus 66, as well as early Christian writings, such as by Tertullian, has cast doubt on the original inclusion of a Martha in this story. Even if it is about sisters Mary and Martha, it would not be the same Mary and Martha that appear in Luke 10 since their hometowns are in completely different locations. The work of Elizabeth Schrader has been instrumental in exploring the early variations in this text (Schrader, Elizabeth (2017). “Was Martha Added to the Fourth Gospel in the Second Century?” Harvard Theological Review, 110(3), 360–392). When I contacted her, she cautioned against including her findings in a translation and suggested instead mentioning them in a footnote. Part of the problem is that her findings in early manuscript evidence only account for verses 1–5 and do not address the presence of Martha in later verses. As I review those verses, there are strange repetitions in the section of verses 20–32. Mary and Martha are said to do identical actions, say identical things. It is not conclusive, but it opens the possibility of a scribe duplicating the verses to make sense of things. For more information, see the recording and its transcript of Diana Butler Bass discussing Schrader’s findings and the impact she sees them making on our understanding of church history: https://dianabutlerbass.substack.com/p/all-the-marys and https://dianabutlerbass.substack.com/p/mary-the-tower.

footnotes.label: e
footnotes.html: Literally, ‘him.’

footnotes.label: f
footnotes.html: The Greek word ide follows ‘Lord’ (kurios) in the text, but it does not have a good English equivalent in this spot. It literally means ‘look’ and is used to indicate the person receiving the message should pay careful attention to what comes next. If it were a warning label or a sign about policy, it could be translated as something like ‘Attention’ or ‘Notice.’ If it were more conversational, ‘look’ could be appropriate, but in a message that your friend is seriously ill, it doesn’t fit into any conventional English pattern.

footnotes.label: g
footnotes.html: The Greek phileo is traditionally translated ‘to love.’ It carries with it a sense of affection, emotional attachment, care, and relational bond. It is shared between friends and family members. It is a different word from the Greek agapao, also traditionally translated as ‘to love,’ which carries a sense of commitment for pursuing benefit for someone, taking care of them.

footnotes.label: h
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘glory’

footnotes.label: i
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘may be glorified’

footnotes.label: j
footnotes.html: Jesus’ response seems possibly connected with Numbers 21:4–9.

footnotes.label: k
footnotes.html: This is agapao, in contrast with phileo in verse 3.

footnotes.label: l
footnotes.html: This word is philos, someone connected by philia (a close, relational bond) or the act of phileo (see verse 3).

footnotes.label: m
footnotes.html: This phrase is a common euphemism for having died, much like ‘passed away’ is used in American culture.

footnotes.label: n
footnotes.html: ‘Restored from his illness’ is translating the Greek sozo. Traditionally, sozo is translated most often as ‘saved.’ In this translation, it most often is translated as ‘liberated.’ The basic meaning is protected or rescued from danger, imprisonment, illness, or harm.

footnotes.label: o
footnotes.html: An Aramaic name meaning ‘twin.’ Possibly, a spelling like ‘Ta’om’ could be a closer equivalent to the Aramaic.

footnotes.label: p
footnotes.html: A Greek name meaning ‘twin.’

footnotes.label: q
footnotes.html: Literally, ‘him’

footnotes.label: r
footnotes.html: Literally, ‘about 15 stades.’ A stade was 607 feet, so the distance was approximately 1.72 miles (since 15 stades is an estimate).

footnotes.label: s
footnotes.html: Or ‘stand up’ or ‘wake up’ or ‘rouse.’ This word anistemi (found also in John 6:39) is the verb form of anastasis (‘rising up’) in John 5:29. There is another verb, histemi, with a related meaning, in fact overlapping quite a bit. However, the prefix an- makes the ‘up’ part of the meaning more emphatic. Anistemi can mean literally to ‘stand up’ or ‘wake up’ and it can mean to ‘stand up’ in the metaphorical sense of taking a stand against oppressors or an army. There are examples of it being used to refer to ‘putting forward’ a champion to do battle in a duel and examples of it being used of driving people out of a land, ‘uprooting’ them from their homes. In John 5:29, the noun form is used of people being woken up from death and uprooted from their tombs and brought forth for either life or assessment (traditionally, judgment). Here, it seems to be related to that concept, being connected with life, as well as hints of those other meanings as well, particularly about rising up against oppression and being put forth as champions in the revolution when God’s reign is fully established at the last day.

footnotes.label: t
footnotes.html: Or ‘the getting up,’ or ‘the waking up/awakening’ or ‘the uprising.’ It would be appropriate even to say ‘the revolution.’ Traditionally, it’s ‘the resurrection.’ Even the English word ‘resurrection’ shares origins with ‘insurrection.’ They have to do with standing up (being ‘erect’). The ‘re-’ in ‘resurrection’ is about returning to a state that was previously experienced. This word is anastasis. Here are the meanings for it listed in The Cambridge Greek Lexicon (2021): 1) act of raising or rising up (from death); 2) rising, awakening, 3) rise (of persons, opposite of ptosis ‘downfall’), 4) erection (of walls), 5) removal (from one’s usual abode); evacuation (of people), 6) withdrawal (of an army), 7) breaking up, adjournment (of an assembly), 8) overthrow, destruction (of a city, country, nation, family). This is the noun form of ‘rise up’ (anistemi).

footnotes.label: u
footnotes.html: Or ‘for.’ The Greek eis can signify movement toward or being for the advantage of something, so it could be ‘come for the benefit/advantage of the world.’

footnotes.label: v
footnotes.html: Or ‘into the world’ or ‘in the world system’

footnotes.label: w
footnotes.html: Literally, ‘that one’ or ‘she’

footnotes.label: x
footnotes.html: Or ‘weep.’ Cuturally, people expressed grief by crying and wailing loudly for others to see.

footnotes.label: y
footnotes.html: There is no scholarly textual criticism that questions this sections authenticity. However, I have bracketed in speculation that it may have been added or modified after the original document began to be copied. The repetition of the events and wording and the inclusion of Martha could all be explained by a scribal decision to make changes. See note on verse 1.

footnotes.label: z
footnotes.html: This word, embrimaomai, is traditionally something like ‘he was deeply moved’ (ESV, NIV, NASB), or ‘he was greatly disturbed’ (NRSV), or ‘he groaned’ (KJV, NKJV). The definition of the word is ‘to scold’ or ‘to warn sternly’ and is related to a word that means ‘to snort with anger.’ In the Greek resources, the only instance of this word used to justify a definition of ‘deeply moved’ is this verse, so the reasoning becomes circular in any argument for that definition. The word is in the ‘middle voice’ which means it is reflexive, directed to oneself. Objections to the translation of ‘he angrily confronted himself’ could be presented based on the idea that any expression of regret or remorse for his actions by Jesus could be construed as being flawed or even as having sinned. However, there is significant biblical precedent for God regretting choices and the course of God’s actions in the Hebrew Bible. In Exodus 34, after the Israelites made a golden calf idol, the text says that God was furious and stated plans to wipe out the people. Moses pleaded on their behalf, “And the Lord changed his mind about the disaster that he planned to bring on his people” (Exodus 32:14 NRSV). The word translated in that verse as ‘changed his mind’ is the same Hebrew word translated about people in other places as ‘repented.’ The better translation is ‘changed his mind.’ That seems to be what Jesus is doing in this verse after seeing the suffering the death caused. He feels an intense emotion about his previous decision to delay and changes his mind about it being the right way to go. There even seems to be something of anger toward himself, not because he was evil but because he wished his actions hadn’t impacted people harmfully.

footnotes.label: aa
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘he was troubled’ or ‘he was greatly distressed.’ However, those translations omit a significant Greek word: ‘himself’ (heauton). It doesn’t just happen to him, he is agitating or upsetting himself. It is the same word to describe what happens to the water in the pool where the man with a 38-year illness hoped to be cleansed when the water was ‘agitated’ or ‘moving’ or ‘stirred up’ in John 5:7. That seems to be what is happening with Jesus. He experiences some anger regarding his previous decision, changes his mind, and stirs himself to action based on that distress. The next verses describe him asking where the body is and moving to the tomb where he outwardly displays his emotions that are being described as ‘in the spirit’ (inward) in this verse before changing his actions to fit his changed mind.

footnotes.label: bb
footnotes.html: This is a different word from the one translated as ‘mourn’ in verses 31 and 33.

footnotes.label: cc
footnotes.html: Literally, ‘this one’ or ‘this man’ or ‘this person.’

footnotes.label: dd
footnotes.html: Literally, ‘this one’ or ‘this man’ or ‘this person.’

footnotes.label: ee
footnotes.html: Literally, ‘being angrily confronted in himself’ or ‘being angrily confronted by himself. This instance of the word is both in the middle voice and includes en heauto, ‘in/by/with himself.’ See footnote in verse 33 for more information.

footnotes.label: ff
footnotes.html: Compare with John 10:1–18.

footnotes.label: gg
footnotes.html: The same word, sunedrion, can be used to refer to ‘the Sanhedrin’ which was the high council of the Judean authorities. For various contextual reasons, this seems to be an unofficial gathering of council members and not an official session of the Sanhedrin.

footnotes.label: hh
footnotes.html: The Greek is laos, where the word ‘lay person’ or ‘laity’ comes from in church contexts, meaning all the people who aren’t clergy. The Greek word just meant all the people as a collective. It could be translated as ‘the people’ or ‘the public’ or ‘the community’ or ‘the crowd,’ etc.

footnotes.label: ii
footnotes.html: The Greek word is ethnos, traditionally translated as ‘nation’ (not as a nation-state in the modern usage, but as a people group, ethnicity) or when it’s plural as ‘Gentiles.’ Here it is talking about the people group descended from Jacob, Israel, as a whole.

footnotes.label: jj
footnotes.html: It is ethnos, ‘people group’ or ‘nation’ or ‘ethnicity’ again here.

footnotes.label: kk
footnotes.html: See Genesis 11:1–9

footnotes.label: ll
footnotes.html: The Greek hagnizo is traditionally translated here as ‘purify themselves’ or ‘ritually cleanse themselves.’ It’s no accident, however, that it looks like hagios, which is traditionally translated as ‘holy’ or when it’s describing people, ‘saints.’ Another definition listed for this word is ‘to consecrate’ or ‘make appropriate for sacred purposes or calling.’

footnotes.label: mm
footnotes.html: Literally, ‘they’ but the context of verses 47–53 and verse 57 indicates who ‘they’ are.

footnotes.label: d
footnotes.html: Or, ‘and his sister Miriam.’ Recent research into the oldest available manuscript of John, Papyrus 66, as well as early Christian writings, such as by Tertullian, has cast doubt on the original inclusion of a Martha in this story. Even if it is about sisters Mary and Martha, it would not be the same Mary and Martha that appear in Luke 10 since their hometowns are in completely different locations. The work of Elizabeth Schrader has been instrumental in exploring the early variations in this text (Schrader, Elizabeth (2017). “Was Martha Added to the Fourth Gospel in the Second Century?” Harvard Theological Review, 110(3), 360–392). When I contacted her, she cautioned against including her findings in a translation and suggested instead mentioning them in a footnote. Part of the problem is that her findings in early manuscript evidence only account for verses 1–5 and do not address the presence of Martha in later verses. As I review those verses, there are strange repetitions in the section of verses 20–32. Mary and Martha are said to do identical actions, say identical things. It is not conclusive, but it opens the possibility of a scribe duplicating the verses to make sense of things. For more information, see the recording and its transcript of Diana Butler Bass discussing Schrader’s findings and the impact she sees them making on our understanding of church history: https://dianabutlerbass.substack.com/p/all-the-marys and https://dianabutlerbass.substack.com/p/mary-the-tower.

footnotes.html: Or ‘stand up’ or ‘wake up’ or ‘rouse.’ This word anistemi (found also in John 6:39) is the verb form of anastasis (‘rising up’) in John 5:29. There is another verb, histemi, with a related meaning, in fact overlapping quite a bit. However, the prefix an- makes the ‘up’ part of the meaning more emphatic. Anistemi can mean literally to ‘stand up’ or ‘wake up’ and it can mean to ‘stand up’ in the metaphorical sense of taking a stand against oppressors or an army. There are examples of it being used to refer to ‘putting forward’ a champion to do battle in a duel and examples of it being used of driving people out of a land, ‘uprooting’ them from their homes. In John 5:29, the noun form is used of people being woken up from death and uprooted from their tombs and brought forth for either life or assessment (traditionally, judgment). Here, it seems to be related to that concept, being connected with life, as well as hints of those other meanings as well, particularly about rising up against oppression and being put forth as champions in the revolution when God’s reign is fully established at the last day.

footnotes.label: z
footnotes.html: This word, embrimaomai, is traditionally something like ‘he was deeply moved’ (ESV, NIV, NASB), or ‘he was greatly disturbed’ (NRSV), or ‘he groaned’ (KJV, NKJV). The definition of the word is ‘to scold’ or ‘to warn sternly’ and is related to a word that means ‘to snort with anger.’ In the Greek resources, the only instance of this word used to justify a definition of ‘deeply moved’ is this verse, so the reasoning becomes circular in any argument for that definition. The word is in the ‘middle voice’ which means it is reflexive, directed to oneself. Objections to the translation of ‘he angrily confronted himself’ could be presented based on the idea that any expression of regret or remorse for his actions by Jesus could be construed as being flawed or even as having sinned. However, there is significant biblical precedent for God regretting choices and the course of God’s actions in the Hebrew Bible. In Exodus 34, after the Israelites made a golden calf idol, the text says that God was furious and stated plans to wipe out the people. Moses pleaded on their behalf, “And the Lord changed his mind about the disaster that he planned to bring on his people” (Exodus 32:14 NRSV). The word translated in that verse as ‘changed his mind’ is the same Hebrew word translated about people in other places as ‘repented.’ The better translation is ‘changed his mind.’ That seems to be what Jesus is doing in this verse after seeing the suffering the death caused. He feels an intense emotion about his previous decision to delay and changes his mind about it being the right way to go. There even seems to be something of anger toward himself, not because he was evil but because he wished his actions hadn’t impacted people harmfully.

footnotes.label: aa
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘he was troubled’ or ‘he was greatly distressed.’ However, those translations omit a significant Greek word: ‘himself’ (heauton). It doesn’t just happen to him, he is agitating or upsetting himself. It is the same word to describe what happens to the water in the pool where the man with a 38-year illness hoped to be cleansed when the water was ‘agitated’ or ‘moving’ or ‘stirred up’ in John 5:7. That seems to be what is happening with Jesus. He experiences some anger regarding his previous decision, changes his mind, and stirs himself to action based on that distress. The next verses describe him asking where the body is and moving to the tomb where he outwardly displays his emotions that are being described as ‘in the spirit’ (inward) in this verse before changing his actions to fit his changed mind.

input.description: Luke 22 in the Liberation and Inclusion Translation (LIT).
paragraphs: 1 The Feast of Unleavened Bread,a which is called Passover, was approaching. 2 The lead priests and scripture scholars were looking for a way to do away with Jesus,b since they were afraid of the people. 3 The Adversaryc went into Judah,d the one called Ish-Kerioth,e who was one of the Twelve. 4 After leaving, he spoke with the lead priests and officers of the temple guard about how to hand him over to them. 5 They were overjoyed and arranged to give him money. 6 He agreed and began looking for an opportunity to hand him over to them away from the crowd.
7 Then the day came for the Feast of Unleavened Bread, on which the Passover lamb was to be slaughtered. 8 Jesusf sent Peter and John,g saying, “Go prepare the Passoverh for us to eat.”
9 “Where do you want us to prepare it?” they asked him.

10 “Look, when you enter the city,” he told them, “Someonei will meet you, carrying a jug of water. Follow him into the house where he goes inside, 11 and tell the owner of the house, ‘The teacher says to you, “Where is the guest roomj where I may eat with my students?”’ 12 He will show you a large, furnished room upstairs. Prepare it there.” 13 When they went, they found it just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover.

14 And when the hour came, Jesusk took a seat at the tablel and the commissioned onesm did so with him. 15 He said to them, “I have longedn to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. 16 You see, I’m telling you, I won’t eat it until it is fully realizedo in God’s Reign.”

17 Then after picking up a cup and giving thanks, he said, “Take this and distribute it among yourselves 18 because, I’m telling you, from now on, I won’t drink any of what is produced by the vine until God’s Reign comes.”

19 Then after taking some bread and giving thanks, he broke it and gave it to them, saying, “This is my body, given for your sake. Do this in remembrance of me.” 20 And likewise, after they ate the meal, he took the cup, saying, “This cup that is poured for your sake is the new covenant connected with my blood. 21 But look, the hand of the one who is handing me over is with me at the table. 22 After all, certainly the Son of Humanityp is going according to what has been appointed, but how pitiableq for that person by whom he is handed over!” 23 Then they began to explore together which of them might be about to do this.

24 There was also contentious rivalry among them about which of them seemed to be the most prominent. 25 So Jesus said to them, “The kings of other peoplesr lord it over them, and those who hold authority over them are called ‘benefactors.’s 26 But not so with you! Instead, the one who is most prominent among you must become like the youngest, and the one who leads like the one who serves. 27 After all, who is more prominent, the one who is seated or the one who serves? Isn’t it the one who is seated? But I am among you as one who serves. 28 You are the ones who have continued to stay with me throughout my times of testing. 29 And I, in turn, pass down a Reign to you, just as my Father passed it down to me, 30 so you may eat and drink at my table in my Reign. You will sit on thrones governingt the twelve tribes of Israel.

31 “Simeon, Simeon,u pay attention! The Adversary has demanded to siftv youw like wheat, 32 but I have pleadedx for you so that your faithfulnessy won’t give out. When you return, support your Family members.”z
33 “Sir,” he said to Jesus,aa “I am ready to go with you to prison and death!”
34 But Jesusbb said, “I’m telling you, Peter, the rooster won’t crow today until you have disowned knowing me three times.”
35 Then he said to them, “When I sent you without a pouch of money or a sack of provisions or even sandals, you didn’t lack for anything, did you?”
“Nothing,” they said.

36 He told them, “But now, whoever has a pouch of money, take it along, and the same with a sack of provisions, and whoever doesn’t have a short swordcc should sell their cloak and buy one. 37 You see,dd I’m telling you that this scripture must be completedee in connection with me: ‘And he was counted as being withff outlawsgg.’hh After all, my part is reaching its completion.”ii
38 Then they said, “Look, sir, here are two swords.”
“It’s enough,”jj he told them.
39 After leaving, Jesuskk went, as usual, to the Mount of Olives, and the students followed him too. 40 When he came to the spot, he said to them, “Pray that you don’t come into a time of testing.”

41 He withdrew from them about a stone’s throw, and kneeling down, he prayed, 42 “Father, if you’re willing, take this cup away from me. However, let what you want happen, not what I want.” ⟦ 43 Then a messengerll from the heavens appeared to him, strengthening him.mm 44 Being in anguish, he prayed more earnestly, and his sweat became like drops of blood falling to the ground. ⟧nn

45 After getting up from prayer, when he came to the students, he found them asleep from grief. 46 “Why are you sleeping?” he said to them. “Get up and pray that you don’too come into a time of testing!”
47 While he was still speaking, suddenly a crowd was there, and the one named Judah, one of the Twelve, was leading them. He approached Jesus to kiss him.pp
48 “Judah,” Jesus said to him, “are you handing over the Son of Humanity with a kiss?”
49 At seeing what was happening, the others around him said, “Sir, should we strike them with swords?” 50 Then one of them struck the person enslaved to the high priest and severed his right ear.
51 “Allow this much!”qq Jesus responded, and he held the man’s ear and restored him.

52 Then Jesus said to the lead priests, officers of the temple guard, and elders who had moved against him, “Did you come out with swords and clubs as if against an armed outlaw? 53 Each day while I was with you in the sacred grounds, you didn’t stretch out your hands against me. But this is your time and the authority of darkness.”rr

54 Seizing him, they took him and brought him to the high priest’s house, but Peter began following at a distance. 55 After they made a fire in the middle of the courtyard and sat down together, Peter sat among them.
56 After seeing him sitting in the firelight and looking intently at him, an enslaved womanss said, “This man was with him too!”
57 But he denied it, saying, “Madam,tt I don’t know him.”
58 A short time later, someone else who saw him stated, “You are one of them too.”
But Peter stated, “Sir,uu I am not.”
59 After about an hour, another person started insisting, “This man was definitely with him too, because he’s also Galilean!”

60 But Peter said, “Sir, I don’t know what you’re talking about!” Right then, as he was still speaking, a rooster crowed. 61 And the Lord turned and looked right at Peter, and Peter remembered what the Lordvv had said, how he had told him, “You will disown me three times before the rooster crows today.” 62 Then he went outside and sobbed with grief.

63 The men who were holding Jesusww began mocking and beating him. 64 After blindfolding him, they asked him repeatedly, “Prophesy! Who hit you?” 65 They kept saying many other things, heaping contemptxx on him.

66 When daylight came, the elders of the people gathered, both the lead priests and the scripture scholars, and they led him away to their Sanhedrin.yy 67 They said, “If you are the Christ,zz tell us.”

But he told them, “If I say it to you, you certainly won’t trust it. 68 Yet if I ask, you certainly won’t answer. 69 From now on, the Son of Humanityaaa will be seated at the right handbbb of the Power of God.”ccc
70 They all said, “Then, are you the Son of God?”ddd
So he told them, “You yourselves are saying that I am.”eee
71 “Why do we need any more testimony? After all, we heard it ourselves from his own mouth!” they said.

footnotes.label: a
footnotes.html: See Exodus 12:1–20 and Deuteronomy 16:1–8.

footnotes.label: b
footnotes.html: The name ‘Jesus’ is added for clarity.

footnotes.label: c
footnotes.html: The word satanas was not a name. It meant ‘adversary’ in the sense of prosecutor or opponent. It carries the meaning of someone who is against another, trying to sabotage their efforts and their wellbeing, and against someone as a plaintiff in court. It is an enemy, but also someone accusing another of wrongdoing, whether truly or falsely. It’s not just about pointing out something bad, but actively moving to cause adversity for someone else. The concept of Ha Shatan in the Hebrew Bible was not the evil archnemesis of God that Christian teaching has turned it into. It was described as a member of the council of spiritual beings whose role was to test people to see how genuine they were. The clearest example of this is in the book of Job.

footnotes.label: d
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘Judas.’ Judas is the English version of the Greek version (Ioudas) of the Hebrew name Yehudah, or ‘Judah’ as it is typically rendered in English translations of the Hebrew Bible.

footnotes.label: e
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘Iscariot.’ It was likely not his name, however. It means ‘man of Kerioth’ which was a city of Moab that was condemned for its actions against Israel, and it was likely used as a label regarding his betrayal of Jesus. See Jeremiah 48:21–47 (especially verses 21–27).

footnotes.label: f
footnotes.html: The name ‘Jesus’ is added for clarity.

footnotes.label: g
footnotes.html: The name ‘John’ is the English version of the Latin version of the Greek transliteration (Ioannes) of the Hebrew name Yohanan or in English translations of the Hebrew Bible, Johanan, which means “God has been gracious” or “My God is gracious.”

footnotes.label: h
footnotes.html: The word is pascha for both Passover and the Passover lamb.

footnotes.label: i
footnotes.html: Many translations use ‘man’ here. The word is anthropos, which just means ‘person’ or ‘human.’ It is sometimes used for a man when distinguishing from a woman, but the usual term for that is aner. What does seem to indicate the person is a male is the pronouns. When a person’s gender is unspecified, Greek uses masculine pronouns, so the grammar leaves open the possibility of a man or woman, but Jesus seems to have someone in mind. In that case, if the person in mind were a woman, he would have used feminine pronouns. There is a common sermon point used about this verse that the strangeness of a man carrying the water was exactly the sign for the students to find the person easily; it does not hold up historically. While women were more frequently the ones responsible for carrying water, it was not so unheard of as the sermon tradition implies.

footnotes.label: j
footnotes.html: This is the same word for ‘guest room’ as in Luke 2:7.

footnotes.label: k
footnotes.html: The name ‘Jesus’ is added for clarity.

footnotes.label: l
footnotes.html: Literally, ‘reclined,’ which was the posture for eating a meal in the culture.

footnotes.label: m
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘apostles.’ The word means ‘someone who is sent to carry out a purpose’ and while it became used in a particular way in the church, it was not an inherently religious word in the Greek language.

footnotes.label: n
footnotes.html: Literally, “I have desired with desire,” mirroring a Hebrew syntax that serves to emphasize intensity.

footnotes.label: o
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘fulfilled.’ It could be translated as something like ‘given a fuller meaning.’ It literally means ‘filled full.’ Much like ‘order fulfillment’ when purchasing an order to be delivered, it means to act on something and bring it to reality in a new way.

footnotes.label: p
footnotes.html: Reference to Ezekiel—“Son of Man” was how Ezekiel referred to himself—and to Daniel 7:13–27. This is one of the loftiest titles Jesus could have used for himself and likely played a key role in accusations against him of attempting to usurp the royal throne. At the same time, though Daniel 7:13–14 connects the “one like a son of humanity” to a kingship with all peoples serving him and that his kingship shall never be destroyed, continuing to verse 27 is the parallel verse that explains it further, and it asserts that “the greatness of the kingdoms under the whole heaven shall be given to the people” as an everlasting kingdom. It also left Jesus with deniability, since he could also claim just to be calling himself a prophet in the tradition of Ezekiel.

footnotes.label: q
footnotes.html: The Greek word ouai is often translated “woe,” but in modern English that sounds vague or archaic. It’s a prophetic outcry expressing both grief and warning, something like “this will end badly for you” or “you’re heading for disaster.” It’s not a curse but a lament for the harm people bring on themselves and each other through hypocrisy and injustice.

footnotes.label: r
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘Gentiles.’ The word ethne literally means ‘nations’ (like ‘nationalities’ not ‘countries’) or ‘people groups’ and is where the English word ‘ethnicity’ comes from. It is usually—but not always—used in the Bible to refer to people groups other than the one the speaker belongs to, so typically to people groups other than Jews since most speakers/authors are Jewish.

footnotes.label: s
footnotes.html: The Greek word here is euergetes, literally “one who does good work.” It was not a description but an honorific bestowed as part of a formal arrangement. Ptolemaic kings and others used it as royal titles, and Greek cities voted to bestow it on the wealthy and powerful, which involved inscribing it in stone, often alongside soter (‘liberator’ or ‘savior’). The benefactor would be someone who donated some object or project or resource to the city. Since the honor of a title never equaled the value of the donation, the city was permanently indebted to the benefactor, owing loyalty and ongoing favors. Most often, the title was given to people who held power over the city in some way, so that the people could stay in the powerful person’s good graces. The especially relevant point for this passage is that the benefactors didn’t give themselves the title; it was bestowed by the people they dominated, binding the people to themselves through a show of generosity that left the people permanently in their debt, not truly being a generous gift at all.

footnotes.label: t
footnotes.html: The Greek here literally says ‘judging’ (krinontes). In biblical contexts, this does not indicate court proceedings and punishment but the role of the judges in the book of Judges. They were the leaders of the community, discerning how to keep the community thriving and protected.

footnotes.label: u
footnotes.html: In English, repeating someone’s name twice can sound patronizing, but in the culture of the text, the repetition of a name in address is always a soft response, indicating compassion or pleading.

footnotes.label: v
footnotes.html: Sifting was an idiom that indicated testing, with the image of determining what is genuine wheat grain and what is empty husk.

footnotes.label: w
footnotes.html: The word ‘you’ is plural, indicating not just Simeon but at least all twelve commissioned ones and maybe all the people present.

footnotes.label: x
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘prayed,’ but the word is more specific than any kind of prayer and isn’t exclusive to prayer. It is the verb for ‘be in need,’ ‘ask,’ or ‘beg,’ expressing strong need and the request to meet the need. It was used in many contexts, not just prayer to God.

footnotes.label: y
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘faith.’ The Greek term pistis communicates meanings such as trust, faithfulness, commitment, and allegiance, reflecting an active, relational trust rather than a static belief. This translation emphasizes an ongoing, reciprocal relationship between trusting someone and committed faithfulness that confirms trustworthiness.

footnotes.label: z
footnotes.html: The word adelphos literally means ‘brother’ or ‘sibling.’ It was also frequently used to refer to ‘cousin’ or ‘relative,’ and even for members of the same ideological or ethnic group. With Jesus’ insistence on a radically inclusive understanding of God’s instruction, it is always pushing further than what already seems to be the most wide-sweeping view people hold. In the New Testament, it comes to be used of anyone who has joined the movement Jesus leads, regardless of gender.

footnotes.label: aa
footnotes.html: The name ‘Jesus’ is added for clarity.

footnotes.label: bb
footnotes.html: The name ‘Jesus’ is added for clarity.

footnotes.label: cc
footnotes.html: The word here is machaira, specifically referring to a short sword or large knife, part of the equipment ordinarily included for travel.

footnotes.label: dd
footnotes.html: The Greek word gar, traditionally translated as ‘for’ and here rendered as ‘you see’ indicates that what comes next is the reason for the instruction just given, the change from taking nothing with them to now being told to bring money, provisions, and swords.

footnotes.label: ee
footnotes.html: Or ‘fulfilled’ or ‘performed’ in the sense of bringing about an end result pointed to by the writing.

footnotes.label: ff
footnotes.html: The quotation of Isaiah 53:12 here is different than the Septuagint Greek that it cites. The Septuagint reads en tois anomois, which means “among the outlaws (or ‘the Torahless’/‘the lawless’).” The Greek of Luke’s text here reads meta anomon, which is something closer to “with outlaws (or ‘people who are Torahless’)” and is closer to the Hebrew ’et-posh’im, ‘with rebels.’ The preposition meta (‘with’) can indicate accompaniment and is the same one used in verse 15 to indicate who would be his Passover companions.

footnotes.label: gg
footnotes.html: The Greek word nomos means ‘law,’ ‘custom,’ or ‘established norm.’ The Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible) used nomos to render torah, and the New Testament writers continued to use it with that sense in many places. It served as a Greek label for that body of writing rather than a rendering of what torah itself means, which is closer to ‘instruction’ or ‘direction.’ The word here is anomos (literally something like ‘no-law’ or, in this context, ‘no-torah’) and it is used in two ways across the New Testament. In one, it describes status: people outside the covenant community and therefore not under Torah, which would essentially be synonymous with ‘Gentile’ and not a statement about behavior. In the other, it describes people whose conduct is contrary to a moral standard, closer to ‘lawless.’ The Hebrew version of the same verse uses posh’im, ‘rebels,’ which leans toward the second sense. This verse is rendered as ‘outlaws’ which can work with both meanings; an outlaw was historically a person placed outside the protection of the law as well as someone who acted against the law, just or unjust.

footnotes.label: hh
footnotes.html: Quotation of Isaiah 53:12

footnotes.label: ii
footnotes.html: The Greek phrase telos echei literally reads ‘has an end’ and is an idiom for being at an end or reaching the end. The root is the same as telesthenai earlier in this verse, translated as ‘be completed.’ It can carry the sense of arriving at an intended goal or simply stopping. Both are likely meant here: what has been written about him arrives at its goal at the same time that he arrives at the end of his work and life. The subject in this sentence, to peri emou, is literally ‘the thing concerning me,’ which is what is rendered here as ‘my part.’

footnotes.label: jj
footnotes.html: The Greek hikanon estin literally means ‘it is enough’ or ‘it is sufficient.’ Many scholars interpret it as Jesus cutting off the conversation because he is exasperated that they misunderstood him, which is somewhat defensible based on several instances of the root word being used in the Septuagint in similar ways; however, those instances (Deuteronomy 3:26; 1 Kings 19:4; 20:11; 1 Chronicles 21:15) are in the imperative: “Let it be enough!” Nothing in the grammar of this verse requires that reading, and it may be that this verse is simply the natural end of an exchange, with Jesus responding to what they said. The confusion happens because Jesus’ followers respond to the part about a packing list for travel, but don’t acknowledge the Isaiah quotation. The reversal of the earlier instruction not to bring supplies is based on that quotation as applied to Jesus, and specifically how Jesus is counted as being with (seemingly as a companion) people outside Torah, i.e. Gentiles. What Jesus imagines they will do with the swords is debated, but whatever it is, later in this chapter, Jesus prevents them from using them for armed resistance.

footnotes.label: kk
footnotes.html: The name ‘Jesus’ is added for clarity.

footnotes.label: ll
footnotes.html: The word angelos means ‘messenger,’ possibly used for spirit beings, but also used for human agents of God (or other people) and sometimes even for natural phenomena. It conveys the meaning of someone authorized to speak—or act—on behalf of another. The reader may faithfully interpret these messengers (acting on God’s behalf) as celestial beings or humans. The word angelos, even for spirit-beings, is a job title, not a ‘species’ classification. The work of Michael S. Heiser is a great source of information on this topic.

footnotes.label: mm
footnotes.html: The Greek word translated as “strengthening him” appears in the Septuagint version of Daniel 10:19 (showing up in the final clause of the following quotation). It is in the context of Daniel in conversation with a heavenly messenger. It reads: Again one in human form touched me and strengthened me. He said, “Do not fear, greatly beloved; you are safe. Be strong and courageous!” When he spoke to me, I was strengthened and said, “Let my lord speak, for you have strengthened me” (Daniel 10:18–19 NRSVue).

footnotes.label: nn
footnotes.html: Luke 22:43–44 is a contested passage, appearing inconsistently among the earliest sources available. Many of the most reliable and earliest manuscripts don’t include it (including Papyrus 75, which is estimated to have been made about 200 CE), and many other early and reliable manuscripts do include it. Patristic writings make reference to it, including Justin Martyr’s Dialogue with Trypho and Irenaeus’ Against Heresies. This translation follows the SBL Greek New Testament, which includes it. The early usage of the passage is relevant for interpreting the significance of it today. Justin Martyr and Irenaeus’ use of it was to argue for the embodiment of Jesus, that he was a real human and not a divine manifestation that only seemed human (a view known as Docetism). The physical vulnerability, the sweat and exhaustion, were presented as the proof. In the late fourth century, Epiphanius of Salamis asserted that the verses were removed by scribes who found them troubling. Others have argued that it was added to provide support for arguments against Docetism. Either way, vulnerability is an essential part of Jesus’ story, and it has always made people uncomfortable, perhaps even to the point of removing it from the text.

footnotes.label: oo
footnotes.html: Or “pray so you don’t”

footnotes.label: pp
footnotes.html: The word is phileo, which literally means ‘love’ or ‘have affection for’ or ‘be attached to’ and can also be used to mean ‘kiss’ as a way to demonstrate affection (though not only romantic or sexual affection as in American culture, but also in friendship or familial affection). It was a common cultural practice for students to kiss their teachers in greeting.

footnotes.label: qq
footnotes.html: The Greek phrase here, eate heos toutou, appears nowhere else in the New Testament and may be unique in all Greek literature. It is a compressed phrase that leaves some of the meaning implicit, and its sense has to be worked out from context. The verb eate is plural and carries two basic meanings: permit and leave alone. The phrase heos toutou means “up to this point” or “this much”; it is uncommon in Greek but does appear in the Septuagint, in Exodus 7:16 and Leviticus 26:18. Most modern English translations render it with the ‘leave alone’ meaning of the verb, along the lines of “No more of this.” This translation renders it with the ‘permit’ meaning. The first one shows Jesus wants the swords to stop, but this translation addresses why the swords should stop: because what is happening is being allowed, just as Jesus prayed, saying, “Father, if you’re willing, take this cup away from me. However, let what you want happen, not what I want” in verse 42. This was the standard English rendering for nearly four centuries. Tyndale translated it as “Soffre ye thus farre forthe” (“suffer ye thus far forth”) in 1534, and subsequent translations kept that interpretation through the Geneva Bible, the King James Version, the American Standard Version and others through the 1920s before the tradition changed with the RSV in 1946 to “No more of this!” A comment preserved in the Greek catena on John, attributed to Apollinaris, calls the line a concession and observes that the word “up to” sets a limit and a check on the sword, reading it as the boundary of Jesus’ concession on swords in verses 36–38. The Gospel of John also makes the connection between the sword and the cup in John 18:11.

footnotes.label: rr
footnotes.html: Compare with Luke 1:79 and Colossians 1:13.

footnotes.label: ss
footnotes.html: While most literally it means ‘girl’ this word (paidiske) was also used for enslaved women. ‘Woman’ is used here based on Peter’s address of the person with gunai in verse 57; it refers to an adult woman, not a child.

footnotes.label: tt
footnotes.html: Literally, the word means ‘woman.’ However, addressing a woman as ‘woman’ in our culture is considered rude, an attempt to put her in her place, especially when done by a man. In the culture of the time, it was a polite way to address someone.

footnotes.label: uu
footnotes.html: The word here is anthrope, literally meaning ‘human’ or ‘person.’ It is the masculine equivalent to gunai as ‘woman’ or ‘madam’ in verse 57. It is a polite address for a male stranger, but it is not deferential like kurios or epistates.

footnotes.label: vv
footnotes.html: The Greek word kurios, when applied to Jesus, can be translated in several ways, including ‘sir,’ ‘master,’ or ‘sovereign.’ Rendering it as ‘Lord’ reflects the reversal of the feudal, patriarchal, and imperial assumptions of imperial and domination-based culture, intended to be a direct challenge to hierarchical power structures. In both Greco-Roman and American history, kurios and ‘lord’ were titles used for slaveowners. As Rev. Dr. Wilda C. Gafney notes, “Lord is a slavery word,” and when used without theological and historical framing, it risks reinscribing the very systems of domination that Jesus came to upend (A Women’s Lectionary for the Whole Church: Year A, Introduction). In the Roman imperial context, kurios was also a title for Caesar—as was soter (‘savior’ or ‘liberator’). The New Testament’s application of kurios to Jesus is thus not only theological but also politically subversive. The Christ of the Christian scriptures is not an overlord but a radically different kind of lord—one who liberates through justice, solidarity, and self-giving love.

footnotes.label: ww
footnotes.html: The name ‘Jesus’ is added for clarity.

footnotes.label: xx
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘blasphemously’ or ‘insulting’ from the Greek word blasphemeo. The Greek word means ‘revile,’ ‘defame,’ or ‘belittle.’

footnotes.label: yy
footnotes.html: Literally, it says ‘their sunedrion’ referring to a council, but based on the people who comprise it, it may refer to the council traditionally called the Sanhedrin in English from the same Greek word. Though there is scholarly debate about the historical reality, the tradition of the Mishnah is that the Sanhedrin was the highest Judean judicial and council body, handling religious, civil, and criminal cases.

footnotes.label: zz
footnotes.html: Christos is the Greek translation of the Hebrew mashiach which has traditionally been transliterated as Messiah (and Christ) but translated would literally be “anointed.” The definition of ‘anointed’ is to be ‘smeared with ointment or oil’ and the biblical significance of anointing is to be selected by God (or a prophet of God) for a special appointment, usually king and sometimes other roles like priest or prophet, and experience a ceremony in which the prophet places oil on the head to signify that appointment.

footnotes.label: aaa
footnotes.html: Reference to Daniel 7:13–14

footnotes.label: bbb
footnotes.html: Reference to Psalm 110:1

footnotes.label: ccc
footnotes.html: The word dunamis literally means ‘power’ or ‘ability.’ It is sometimes used in place of referring to God directly, as was often the customary practice of the time. In Mark 14:62, it has this phrase without “of God” following. Luke seems to reference the same statement by Jesus but likely added “of God” for clarity for his non-Jewish audience.

footnotes.label: ddd
footnotes.html: “The Son of God” was a nickname for the emperor, a title taken on originally by Augustus Caesar, the son of Julius Caesar who was worshiped as divine, and was then used by other, subsequent emperors.

footnotes.label: eee
footnotes.html: Compare with Luke 4:41, where demons are the ones naming him as Christ and Son of God.

expected.title: Luke 22
expected.description: Luke 22 in the Liberation and Inclusion Translation (LIT).
expected.text: The Feast of Unleavened Bread, which is called Passover, was approaching. The lead priests and scripture scholars were looking for a way to do away with Jesus, since they were afraid of the people. The Adversary went into Judah, the one called Ish-Kerioth, who was one of the Twelve. After leaving, he spoke with the lead priests and officers of the temple guard about how to hand him over to them. They were overjoyed and arranged to give him money. He agreed and began looking for an opportunity to hand him over to them away from the crowd. Then the day came for the Feast of Unleavened Bread, on which the Passover lamb was to be slaughtered. Jesus sent Peter and John, saying, “Go prepare the Passover for us to eat.” “Where do you want us to prepare it?” they asked him. “Look, when you enter the city,” he told them, “Someone will meet you, carrying a jug of water. Follow him into the house where he goes inside, and tell the owner of the house, ‘The teacher says to you, “Where is the guest room where I may eat with my students?”’ He will show you a large, furnished room upstairs. Prepare it there.” When they went, they found it just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover. And when the hour came, Jesus took a seat at the table and the commissioned ones did so with him. He said to them, “I have longed to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. You see, I’m telling you, I won’t eat it until it is fully realized in God’s Reign.” Then after picking up a cup and giving thanks, he said, “Take this and distribute it among yourselves because, I’m telling you, from now on, I won’t drink any of what is produced by the vine until God’s Reign comes.” Then after taking some bread and giving thanks, he broke it and gave it to them, saying, “This is my body, given for your sake. Do this in remembrance of me.” And likewise, after they ate the meal, he took the cup, saying, “This cup that is poured for your sake is the new covenant connected with my blood. But look, the hand of the one who is handing me over is with me at the table. After all, certainly the Son of Humanity is going according to what has been appointed, but how pitiable for that person by whom he is handed over!” Then they began to explore together which of them might be about to do this. There was also contentious rivalry among them about which of them seemed to be the most prominent. So Jesus said to them, “The kings of other peoples lord it over them, and those who hold authority over them are called ‘benefactors.’ But not so with you! Instead, the one who is most prominent among you must become like the youngest, and the one who leads like the one who serves. After all, who is more prominent, the one who is seated or the one who serves? Isn’t it the one who is seated? But I am among you as one who serves. You are the ones who have continued to stay with me throughout my times of testing. And I, in turn, pass down a Reign to you, just as my Father passed it down to me, so you may eat and drink at my table in my Reign. You will sit on thrones governing the twelve tribes of Israel. “Simeon, Simeon, pay attention! The Adversary has demanded to sift you like wheat, but I have pleaded for you so that your faithfulness won’t give out. When you return, support your Family members.” “Sir,” he said to Jesus, “I am ready to go with you to prison and death!” But Jesus said, “I’m telling you, Peter, the rooster won’t crow today until you have disowned knowing me three times.” Then he said to them, “When I sent you without a pouch of money or a sack of provisions or even sandals, you didn’t lack for anything, did you?” “Nothing,” they said. He told them, “But now, whoever has a pouch of money, take it along, and the same with a sack of provisions, and whoever doesn’t have a short sword should sell their cloak and buy one. You see, I’m telling you that this scripture must be completed in connection with me: ‘And he was counted as being with outlaws.’ After all, my part is reaching its completion.” Then they said, “Look, sir, here are two swords.” “It’s enough,” he told them. After leaving, Jesus went, as usual, to the Mount of Olives, and the students followed him too. When he came to the spot, he said to them, “Pray that you don’t come into a time of testing.” He withdrew from them about a stone’s throw, and kneeling down, he prayed, “Father, if you’re willing, take this cup away from me. However, let what you want happen, not what I want.” Then a messenger from the heavens appeared to him, strengthening him. Being in anguish, he prayed more earnestly, and his sweat became like drops of blood falling to the ground. After getting up from prayer, when he came to the students, he found them asleep from grief. “Why are you sleeping?” he said to them. “Get up and pray that you don’t come into a time of testing!” While he was still speaking, suddenly a crowd was there, and the one named Judah, one of the Twelve, was leading them. He approached Jesus to kiss him. “Judah,” Jesus said to him, “are you handing over the Son of Humanity with a kiss?” At seeing what was happening, the others around him said, “Sir, should we strike them with swords?” Then one of them struck the person enslaved to the high priest and severed his right ear. “Allow this much!” Jesus responded, and he held the man’s ear and restored him. Then Jesus said to the lead priests, officers of the temple guard, and elders who had moved against him, “Did you come out with swords and clubs as if against an armed outlaw? Each day while I was with you in the sacred grounds, you didn’t stretch out your hands against me. But this is your time and the authority of darkness.” Seizing him, they took him and brought him to the high priest’s house, but Peter began following at a distance. After they made a fire in the middle of the courtyard and sat down together, Peter sat among them. After seeing him sitting in the firelight and looking intently at him, an enslaved woman said, “This man was with him too!” But he denied it, saying, “Madam, I don’t know him.” A short time later, someone else who saw him stated, “You are one of them too.” But Peter stated, “Sir, I am not.” After about an hour, another person started insisting, “This man was definitely with him too, because he’s also Galilean!” But Peter said, “Sir, I don’t know what you’re talking about!” Right then, as he was still speaking, a rooster crowed. And the Lord turned and looked right at Peter, and Peter remembered what the Lord had said, how he had told him, “You will disown me three times before the rooster crows today.” Then he went outside and sobbed with grief. The men who were holding Jesus began mocking and beating him. After blindfolding him, they asked him repeatedly, “Prophesy! Who hit you?” They kept saying many other things, heaping contempt on him. When daylight came, the elders of the people gathered, both the lead priests and the scripture scholars, and they led him away to their Sanhedrin. They said, “If you are the Christ, tell us.” But he told them, “If I say it to you, you certainly won’t trust it. Yet if I ask, you certainly won’t answer. From now on, the Son of Humanity will be seated at the right hand of the Power of God.” They all said, “Then, are you the Son of God?” So he told them, “You yourselves are saying that I am.” “Why do we need any more testimony? After all, we heard it ourselves from his own mouth!” they said.

footnotes.label: i
footnotes.html: Many translations use ‘man’ here. The word is anthropos, which just means ‘person’ or ‘human.’ It is sometimes used for a man when distinguishing from a woman, but the usual term for that is aner. What does seem to indicate the person is a male is the pronouns. When a person’s gender is unspecified, Greek uses masculine pronouns, so the grammar leaves open the possibility of a man or woman, but Jesus seems to have someone in mind. In that case, if the person in mind were a woman, he would have used feminine pronouns. There is a common sermon point used about this verse that the strangeness of a man carrying the water was exactly the sign for the students to find the person easily; it does not hold up historically. While women were more frequently the ones responsible for carrying water, it was not so unheard of as the sermon tradition implies.

footnotes.label: s
footnotes.html: The Greek word here is euergetes, literally “one who does good work.” It was not a description but an honorific bestowed as part of a formal arrangement. Ptolemaic kings and others used it as royal titles, and Greek cities voted to bestow it on the wealthy and powerful, which involved inscribing it in stone, often alongside soter (‘liberator’ or ‘savior’). The benefactor would be someone who donated some object or project or resource to the city. Since the honor of a title never equaled the value of the donation, the city was permanently indebted to the benefactor, owing loyalty and ongoing favors. Most often, the title was given to people who held power over the city in some way, so that the people could stay in the powerful person’s good graces. The especially relevant point for this passage is that the benefactors didn’t give themselves the title; it was bestowed by the people they dominated, binding the people to themselves through a show of generosity that left the people permanently in their debt, not truly being a generous gift at all.

footnotes.label: gg
footnotes.html: The Greek word nomos means ‘law,’ ‘custom,’ or ‘established norm.’ The Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible) used nomos to render torah, and the New Testament writers continued to use it with that sense in many places. It served as a Greek label for that body of writing rather than a rendering of what torah itself means, which is closer to ‘instruction’ or ‘direction.’ The word here is anomos (literally something like ‘no-law’ or, in this context, ‘no-torah’) and it is used in two ways across the New Testament. In one, it describes status: people outside the covenant community and therefore not under Torah, which would essentially be synonymous with ‘Gentile’ and not a statement about behavior. In the other, it describes people whose conduct is contrary to a moral standard, closer to ‘lawless.’ The Hebrew version of the same verse uses posh’im, ‘rebels,’ which leans toward the second sense. This verse is rendered as ‘outlaws’ which can work with both meanings; an outlaw was historically a person placed outside the protection of the law as well as someone who acted against the law, just or unjust.

footnotes.label: ii
footnotes.html: The Greek phrase telos echei literally reads ‘has an end’ and is an idiom for being at an end or reaching the end. The root is the same as telesthenai earlier in this verse, translated as ‘be completed.’ It can carry the sense of arriving at an intended goal or simply stopping. Both are likely meant here: what has been written about him arrives at its goal at the same time that he arrives at the end of his work and life. The subject in this sentence, to peri emou, is literally ‘the thing concerning me,’ which is what is rendered here as ‘my part.’

footnotes.label: jj
footnotes.html: The Greek hikanon estin literally means ‘it is enough’ or ‘it is sufficient.’ Many scholars interpret it as Jesus cutting off the conversation because he is exasperated that they misunderstood him, which is somewhat defensible based on several instances of the root word being used in the Septuagint in similar ways; however, those instances (Deuteronomy 3:26; 1 Kings 19:4; 20:11; 1 Chronicles 21:15) are in the imperative: “Let it be enough!” Nothing in the grammar of this verse requires that reading, and it may be that this verse is simply the natural end of an exchange, with Jesus responding to what they said. The confusion happens because Jesus’ followers respond to the part about a packing list for travel, but don’t acknowledge the Isaiah quotation. The reversal of the earlier instruction not to bring supplies is based on that quotation as applied to Jesus, and specifically how Jesus is counted as being with (seemingly as a companion) people outside Torah, i.e. Gentiles. What Jesus imagines they will do with the swords is debated, but whatever it is, later in this chapter, Jesus prevents them from using them for armed resistance.
